runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (now about $92, down from $115 in late October), a yen close to the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield back above 5% with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

Update · Thu 12 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers Wednesday 11 Nov in Asia and the US close)
Chip stocks bounce back as CoreWeave calms AI-spending fears; oil edges up as Iran denies talks

AI and chip stocks rebounded on Wednesday after CoreWeave's results eased worries about AI spending. The chip index rose about 7% and the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620, now about 2.5% below its record. NVIDIA recovered about 3.5% after two days of losses. Asia had already rallied on chip demand: Korea +2.4%, Taiwan +3.6% and Japan +1.3%. Brent rose about 1% to roughly $92.5 as Iran denied any talks with the US and attacks on tankers continued. Gold slipped about 1% to just under $4,000. US bond markets were shut for Veterans Day, and a December Fed hike is still fully priced. No fund rating changes.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
AI and chip stocks bounced back.

CoreWeave jumped more than 20% after its results; it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over the next three months and says it plans no more expensive debt through 2027. The Philadelphia chip index rose about 7%, with Micron up about 12%, Sandisk about 15% and Dell about 13% late in the session (Reuters). NVIDIA rose about 3.5–3.8% after losing roughly $430–480bn of market value over the previous two days, though Baird cut its rating to Neutral. Microsoft fell about 2.5%. The S&P 500 ended about 1.3% higher at roughly 7,620, the Nasdaq about 1.6% and the Dow about 0.5%.

A relief day for the AI-heavy funds (6, 3, 4, 13, 19) and for Asian chip exposure (24, 22). CoreWeave avoiding costly new debt is mildly reassuring for AI borrowing inside the credit funds (20, 21). One good results day does not end the sell-off: NVIDIA's results later this month remain the bigger test.
Asia rallied on chip demand; SoftBank slipped.

Korea's KOSPI rose 2.4% to 5,365.75 as SK Hynix gained 5.4% and Samsung 3.4%. Taiwan rose 3.6%, with TSMC up 3.1%; its board approved up to $1bn of investment in Anthropic and OpenAI. Japan's Nikkei rose 1.3% to 61,248.59, but SoftBank closed 0.4% lower after a quarterly net loss of about ¥1.1 trillion (about $7bn). Hong Kong fell 0.7%, Shanghai rose 0.6% and Australia 0.3% (AP). The dollar edged up to 158.85 yen.

Good for Asia ex-Japan (24) and emerging markets (22), which hold Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC, and for Japan (27). The Pacific fund (7) was flatter, with Hong Kong down and Australia slightly up. The yen is still close to the 160 level that has triggered intervention, a risk for the yen funds (11, 27).
Oil edged up as Iran denied talks; gold slipped.

Brent rose about 1.1% to roughly $92.5 a barrel, recovering from a 10-week low. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei denied any negotiations with the US and said the Strait of Hormuz stays shut until Iran's seven conditions are met; Iran also said it will not give up its enriched nuclear material. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers caught fire after hitting mines on Tuesday, and monitors count at least 37 attacks on ships in and near the strait so far in November, the most of any month in the war. Trump and Rubio said new strikes are not needed. Saudi output rose 26% in October to 10.56m barrels a day. Spot gold fell about 1% to just under $4,000 an ounce.

Oil is stuck in the low $90s: deal hopes pull it down, while attacks and Iran's hard line hold it up. That matters for the commodity fund (12) and UK energy shares (8), and for oil importers in Europe (5), Japan (27) and Asia (23). Gold below $4,000 keeps pressure on the gold miners fund (1).
Rates: bond markets closed, hike bets unchanged.

US bond markets were shut for Veterans Day, leaving the 10-year yield near 5.0% from Tuesday. CME FedWatch showed a December quarter-point hike fully priced and about 13% odds of a half point (Reuters). Fed Governor Bowman said there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%. BofA called the S&P 500 the most crowded equity trade in the world.
No relief yet for the bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) or listed real estate (2); Friday's producer-price report is the next test. Cash and money market funds (14) keep benefiting from higher rates.
Coming up (Manila):

US October producer prices Fri 13 Nov, 9:30 pm; Japan Q3 GDP Mon 16 Nov; Fed minutes Thu 19 Nov, early morning; Anthropic's market debut expected around 19–20 Nov, at $70–78 a share; NVIDIA results late November; US November jobs report Fri 4 Dec, 9:30 pm; Fed decision 8–9 Dec, with a hike fully priced.

Another hot price report would raise the odds of a half-point hike and hurt the bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) and tech (6, 13). Weak Japanese GDP would complicate a Bank of Japan hike and weigh on the yen funds (27, 11).

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit

1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. Japan had already spent ¥11.7 trillion defending the yen in April–May. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. In the week to 6 Nov the dollar traded between about 157.3 and 158.8 yen; hawkish Bank of Japan minutes and the stock rout helped the yen, but the strong US jobs report pushed the dollar back to the mid-158s. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. After the 3 Nov US election, Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62 on 4 Nov as markets priced pressure to end the war, and it ended the week of 6 Nov at $98.32, down about 16%, its steepest weekly fall since 2020. On 8 Nov the US launched "Task Force Iron Gate" to curb Iran's trade over land and the Caspian Sea, and on 9 Nov Brent fell about 5% to roughly $93–94, its lowest since 31 Aug. On 10 Nov Brent briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August, ending near $91.8, after Trump said the war was militarily effectively over. On 11 Nov Iran denied any talks with the US and said the strait stays shut until its conditions are met; monitors counted at least 37 attacks on ships so far in November, the most of any month in the war, and Brent rose about 1% to roughly $92.5. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%), and markets briefly priced about 50% odds of a second Fed hike this week. The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002, and Pimco's CIO has said 6% is possible. On 6 Nov a strong October jobs report (165,000 jobs against about 65,000 expected, unemployment 4.1%) lifted the 2-year yield to 4.51% and the 10-year to 4.86%, and pushed CME odds of a December hike to about 77%. On 9 Nov China's October factory prices rose 5.7% from a year earlier, a four-year high, and CME odds of a December Fed hike were still above 80% even as oil fell. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 11 Nov US bond markets were shut for Veterans Day; CME odds still showed a December hike fully priced, with about 13% odds of a half point, and Governor Bowman said there is still work to do on inflation. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed.

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 11 Nov CoreWeave said it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over three months and plans no more expensive debt through 2027; its shares jumped more than 20% and the chip index about 7%.

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level, then rebounded to $3,957 on 2 Nov and $4,070 on 4 Nov. It gained about 4.5% in the week to 6 Nov, its best week since August, ending near $4,050–4,080. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias.

Holdings, returns, AI exposure and liquidity
Buying in a sell-off
If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: the S&P 500 closed at about 7,620 on Wed 11 Nov, roughly 2.5% below its record, after chip stocks rebounded. It is still above the −5% level (~7,430), which is about 2.5% lower. The −10% level (~7,040) is about 7.6% lower.

runs.text: Nobody can pick the bottom. Splitting purchases across the three levels means you are never all-in too early or left with all your cash. The dot-com and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rallies on the way down.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.
Buying a dip means
switching
part of an existing balance (for example, from Insight into Developed World). Changing only where new money goes keeps buying at every level automatically, but does not move what is already invested.

are my judgement, not model output or forecasts.
Volatility 1–7
(shown as "Risk 1–7" in the earlier version) is my rating on the familiar SRI scale for how much each fund's price swings; it is not the official KID rating.
Other key risks
are non-AI threats backed by news from 4–26 October 2026: currencies, oil, inflation and rates, sovereign debt, geopolitics and credit. Each is rated Low, Medium or High for that fund.
Overall risk

combines AI exposure, those other risks and volatility into one judgement, on a scale from Very low to Very high, for an investor whose spending currency is the US dollar. Funds 11 and 15 carry a note because their risk is much lower in their own currency. These ratings are my judgement and will change with the news; the dates to watch are listed under Other risks.
This page is research to inform your own decision. I am not a licensed financial adviser, and the right mix depends on your horizon, currency and other assets.
